title: Sturge weber syndrome: A case report
case_prompt: A 14-year-old boy was brought to the emergency department after a 4-minute generalized tonic–clonic seizure with frothing and tongue biting, followed by postictal confusion. He had a similar seizure at age 10 treated with levetiracetam, which was stopped by his parents 6 months ago. He had no history of headaches, stroke-like events, or head trauma, and no family history of seizures. On examination, vital signs were normal. A 2-cm laceration was noted on the lateral tongue. There was a reddish discoloration on the right side of the face, involving the forehead, scalp, eyebrow, and upper eyelid; this port-wine stain had been present since birth. Neurologic examination, including cognition, was normal. Ophthalmologic examination showed no glaucoma. Routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. A head CT scan demonstrated tram-track cortical calcifications in the right temporal and occipital lobes without volume loss. Brain MRI with contrast revealed curvilinear cortical and subcortical calcifications in the right posterior temporal lobe, prominent leptomeningeal enhancement, and an enlarged ipsilateral choroid plexus.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. The combination of a congenital V1-distribution port-wine stain, seizures, cortical calcifications, and leptomeningeal enhancement supports the diagnosis — “Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain disclosed curvilinear cortical and subcortical calcifications in the right posterior temporal lobe, accompanied by notable leptomeningeal enhancement and prominent ipsilateral choroid plexus.”
2. Other vascular malformation syndromes were considered — “Differential diagnoses include Maffuci’s syndrome, Von Hippel Lindau disease, Rendu-Osler-Weber syndrome, angio-osteodystrophy syndrome and Klippel Trenaumy-Weber syndrome.”
